title: Chemical Equilibrium

cards.b: Many reactions do not run to completion. They reach a balance where products form and revert at the same rate. This equilibrium decides how much ammonia a plant makes, how your blood stays at the right pH and why fizzy drinks go flat when opened.

In a reversible reaction (written with a double arrow, ⇌) the forward and reverse reactions both occur. At equilibrium their rates are equal. Concentrations stay constant, but nothing has stopped: molecules keep reacting both ways, like a busy escalator with equal people going up and down.

Example: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.

For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the constant is

Kc

Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b)

Brackets mean concentration in mol/L. For ammonia: Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3).

  • Large K (much greater than 1): mostly products.
  • Small K (much less than 1): mostly reactants.
  • K depends only on temperature.

Henri Le Chatelier, 1884: if you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts to partly undo the disturbance.

  • Add reactant: shifts toward products.
  • Remove product: shifts toward products.
  • Raise pressure: shifts to the side with fewer gas molecules.
  • Raise temperature: favours the endothermic direction.
  • Catalyst: no shift, only reaches equilibrium faster.

cards.h: The Haber process as a puzzle
cards.b: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, exothermic (about -92 kJ per mole of reaction). Fritz Haber proved the method in 1909 and Carl Bosch scaled it up industrially by 1913.

A fizzy drink holds CO2 in solution: CO2(g) ⇌ CO2(aq). Opening the bottle drops pressure, so CO2 escapes. Blood contains a CO2 / bicarbonate buffer system keeping pH near 7.4. Oceans absorb CO2 forming carbonic acid, the root of ocean acidification.

A + B ⇌ C. At equilibrium [A] = 0.20, [B] = 0.10, [C] = 0.40 mol/L.

Kc = [C] / ([A][B]) = 0.40 / (0.20 x 0.10) = 20. Products are favoured.

Le Chatelier check: if more B is added, equilibrium shifts forward, giving more C until Kc returns to 20.

• Equal concentrations are not equilibrium. Equal rates are.
  • Catalysts do not change K or the yield, only the speed.
  • Equilibrium does not mean the reaction has stopped.
  • Pure solids and liquids are left out of K.

India's urea industry relies on ammonia made by high-pressure equilibrium chemistry. Cooperative giants like IFFCO (founded 1967) and many public-sector units run plants where engineers tune pressure, temperature and catalysts using exactly these principles to maximise yield and cut energy use. Shifting to green ammonia from renewable hydrogen is now a stated national goal.

• Equilibrium: forward rate equals reverse rate; concentrations constant.
  • Kc = products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient; depends only on temperature.
  • Le Chatelier: systems oppose a disturbance.

Think about it

1. Why use a compromise temperature in the Haber process?

2. Why does warm soda go flat faster than cold soda?

o: Forward and reverse rates are equal
